newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr ekes out thin range, flows frugal.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr ekes out thin range, flows frugal.

text.p: The Australian dollar sat through a frugal trading range Tuesday with the market starved of fresh flows, or the news to generate them.

Today's monthly meeting of the Reserve Bank board had been pre-empted by an impromptu ringaround a week ago to sanction Wednesday's official rate cut. There were no economic data of note until jobs figures on Thursday and they were so notoriously volatile few traders dared bet on the outcome.
Consulting the technical tea leaves only yielded a period of sideways consolidation with the bearish implications of the failed rally to 75 cents, balanced by the bounce from US$0.7360.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was idling at US$0.7392/97 having started at US$0.7405/10 from US$0.7390/95 late here Monday. That was up on its US$0.7365 trough but a long way from last week's US$0.7505 high.

The failure to follow through on that short covering rally and the resulting lapse into its old trading band has left the market lost for direction. Technicals were mostly bearish following the cut below US$0.7440 and argued for an extension of the five month-old downtrend to at least US$0.7250 and possibly US$0.7070. But dealers remembered how impressive bids had been around US$0.7330 and were not keen to chase the currency lower.
There was a little more action on the crosses where the dollar closed at a fresh five year high on the mark at 1.3808/21 having climbed from 1.3778/93 late here Monday.
It was firmer on the yen at 87.62/72 from 87.47/57 and at 58.1 in trade weighted terms from a previous 58.0.

But it lost ground to the Kiwi after New Zealand jobs data proved less weak than expected and monetary conditions there tightened. The unemployment rate edged up to 6.7 percent in June from 6.5 percent but market forecasts had been for 6.9 percent.
The Kiwi rose to US$0.6454/59 from US$0.6425/30 while the A$ eased to NZ$1.1431/47 from NZ$1.1505/25.
Labour data are much on the mind of local traders who suspect a weak employment report on Thursday could start the speculation of yet another easing in monetary policy.

Analysts expect employment to rise around 25,000 in July, more than twice June's 11,900 gain. But still the two months added together would not make up for May's 40,300 drop, and the unemployment rate was likely to nudge up from 8.5 percent as more people went looking for work.
Most analysts reckoned there was enough stimulus in the pipeline -- the 0.5 point cut in official rates to 5.0 percent was the fifth in a year -- to promote a pickup in growth.

But signs of economic strength had mainly been confined to leading indicators so far and the inflation outlook was so favourable the central bank might feel there was little risk in taking further insurance on a recovery.

The bank's board held its monthly meeting today but the event has lost much of its importance given the RBA explicitly severed the link between meetings and the timing of changes in policy in the statement accompanying last week's easing.
Elsewhere, commodity prices have offered some relief to A$ bulls in the last couple of weeks as the influential commodity Research Bureau index of futures contracts rallied strongly.
After plunging almost nine percent to a two-year low of 232.01 in early July the index had bounced all the way to 245.26 by Monday, regaining crucial support at 236.00 in the process.
Nevertheless, that only put it in the middle of the range held all year and analysts were still waiting for the sustained rise they had thought would result from stronger world growth.

It was those expectations which still led some to forecast a firmer A$ by year-end -- the dollar has historically shown a close correlation to the price of commodities since they make up over 60 percent of Australian exports.
